FOUR MEN FOUND DEAD,
Two Hanging to a Tree and Two Shot Through.
The startling news reached the city yesterday that four dead men were found in Elm bottom yesterday morning, two of whom were hanging by their necks from limbs and two others pierced with bullets. The two hanging were about half a mile from the two found that were shot. The place is near the line of the Missouri Pacific road north of Lewisville. C. W. Hallsell, a young man, arrived in the city during the day and verified the rumor, yet the mail agent who came in on the 4 o'clock train from Denton, stated to a HERALD reporter that he had heard nothing of any bodies being found. Young Halsell says that Mrs. McWorter, who resides near Lewisville, gave him what little information he had, which was in substance as given above. None of the bodies, which were dressed in cow-boy style, were identified, yet one of the shot men was recognized as a party who had been seen the previous day at Caruth's ranch near where the remains had been found. Carter, a relative of Carter of Sam Bass fame, who is supposed to be one of the gang found dead, had been captured Tuesday night while trying to rob a passenger train on the Missouri Pacific road, several miles this side of Denton, but that he declared his ignorance as to whom the dead men were. The rumor lacks confirmation and is not credited.

Miss Mills, aged 17, Emma Oglesby, an orphan, aged 16, and Mary Jones, aged 14, all employed by Mr. Brown, who keeps a boarding-house, bought 25 cents' worth of arsenic, June 21, divided it into three doses, and swallowed it. MORE LYNCHING.
MORE LYNCHING.
The usually staid and law abiding parish of Bossier has been disgraced by a lynching affair. Tuesday night of last week a party of about a dozen men gained admission to the jailor's bedroom, obtained possession of the keys of the jail by threats, entered the prison and brought out Henry Solomon, a colored man, whom they hanged just outside the building. An inquest was held and, as usual, the jailor, his assistants and the prisoners incarcerated with Solomon all testified that they did not recognize any of the lynchers, though it does not even appear from the evidence, as reported by the Banner, that the law breakers were masked or disguised in any way.

Solomon had been imprisoned on a charge of mule stealing, and was thought to be a bad character, but it is not urged that he was ever convicted of any offense. During the night of the 10th inst., in company with one Jack Chapman, a white man convicted of murder and sentenced to death, Solomon broke out of jail and fled. The pair were subsequently captured and returned to prison. The night of the lynching the floor of the cell occupied by Solomon was found to be burning, and the prisoner is said to have acknowledged that he started the fire with the intention of effecting an escape. We presume this was the overt act that justified the lynchers, in their own estimation, in murdering a man who had never been convicted of any breach of law and was entitled to the legal presumption of innocence until proven guilty.

The Bossier Banner regrets the occurrence and says "such a method of inflicting justice is undoubtedly dangerous," but expresses "the candid belief that the legal quibbles and quirks so freely used in defense of criminals everywhere, now-a-days, is answerable for this state of affairs."

The excuse is a very weak one in this instance, for no attempt had yet been made under the forms of law to bring Solomon to an account for his alleged misdeeds. If the night-prowling jayhawkers were actuated by the fear that a criminal would escape punishment unless they inflicted it outside the pale of the law, why did they select a poor darkkey, never convicted of crime and only accused of stealing a mule, passing by a white murderer who had been duly tried and pronounced guilty and who is endeavoring to evade the penalty of his great crime—one of the most serious and infamous in the category of lawless deeds—by "legal quibbles and quirks?" Jake Chapman is prosecuting an appeal before the Supreme Court, and should any irregularity be discovered in the proceedings in his case, he will be granted a new trial and will stand the chance of securing an acquittal or of making a second and more successful attempt to escape by breaking jail and fleeing to parts unknown. If Solomon's effort to regain his liberty by flight is taken as a confession of guilt, the same assumption must apply in Chapman's case, even signifying the fact that the latter had been duly tried and convicted, while the former had never been accorded the right of a trial.

It certainly appears on the face of the record that the Bossier lynchers made a very marked distinction between white tweedle-dee and colored tweedle-dum, and in three out of every four instances of lynching in Louisiana the same tendency is to be observed. On the 19th of December last, J. B. Weisinger, a plante, near Brown's station, Alabama, a man 60 years of age, was brutally murdered in his own house, half a dozen negroes being supposed to have had a hand in it. Two of them named Bill Ludlow and Al. Weisinger, were finally brought to trial and convicted, and on the 31st of March executed. Yesterday at 9 o'clock Justice Gregg called the jury of inquest, in the case of the man killed in the first ward Monday night, and a thorough and searching investigation as to the facts governing the killing was had. The evidence in the case is, in substance, just about what was stated in yesterday's STATESMAN, and is as follows:

THE EVIDENCE.

Captain J. L. Watts, being sworn, testified: Last night about 11 o'clock I was informed, while on duty, that two white men had assaulted a colored man near Bertram's store, and that the unknown parties had gone towards the first ward. I went with the colored man that way, looking for the men, and came upon them in a house of ill-fame, known as Sallie Daggett's. Two heres were hitched in front, and recognized as the horses ridden by the men. I had a full description of the men. As I came to the gate I met Billie McCllan, and when inside I asked him to assist me in the arrest. Two of the girls, upon inquiry, said the men in question were in the wine room. I then crossed the little platform in the rear, leading to the said wine room, and met the two men aforesaid. I, approaching them, took each by the arm, saying: "Gentlemen, consider yourselves under arrest." Instantly both jumped back, drawing their pistols. I knocked the deceased off the steps, he having a pistol in his hand, and whirling to grab the other, one Jeff Ake, now present, the latter fired at me, striking me in the side. We began wrestling, and I observed the deceased again on his feet and advancing, aiming his pistol at me with both hands. I hallowed to McCllan, "For God's sake kill him!" He (McC.) said he had no pistol, and, upon my request, quickly took mine from my belt, as I could not get away from Jeff Ake. McCllan fired upon the deceased. When I succeeded in getting Jeff Ake to the door and throwing him I learned from McCllan that the deceased was shot. The prisoner had fired a second shot, ineffectually, at me, while the tussle was continuing. Upon the appearance of the city marshal, in answer to summons through others, coming upon the scene, I left with Jeff Ake in custody. Above happened on 2nd day of January, A. D., 1883.

J. L. Watts.

R. J. Stewart, being sworn, testifies: When I came into the hall, Officer Watts had a man down, and one McClellan was standing near by, who said shut the door and don't let anybody in. He further said, there might be some more of them, and, that one was down outside, and he thought was dying. During this Officer Watts still held Jeff Ake down. After shutting the door, I went out through the back door and found the deceased lying on the gallery in a dying condition, and I remained as policeman to keep the crowd up, until the marshal arrived. The doctor came, and Officer Watts left with Jeff Ake. I heard firing, and went to see what was the matter.

R. J. STEWART.

Ike Johnson, being sworn, testifies: Last night near eleven o'clock, I was going home, near Bertram's old store, with my wife, and met two white men in the road, and to keep from being run over, I gave the road, saying, to Jeff Ake, who I now recognize as the man, "Look out, mister, this may cost you something." AN INTERVIEW WITH JEFF AKES IN JAIL.

A STATESMAN reporter called at the jail yesterday afternoon at 5 o'clock, and requested an interview with Jeff Akes, when Captain A. Denny, the efficient keeper of the prison, courteously showed him up to the cell where the prisoner is confined.

HIS APPEARANCH.

The prisoner is a man of probably thirty-five years of age, five feet six inches high, rather sparely made, and has light or sandy hair. His eye is dull and uninteresting, but the whole contour of his face, as well as his decided expression and precise manner, would seem to indicate decision of character. In fact, his very looks betoken a "bad man," when aroused or under the influence of drink. When informed that a reporter wished to see him, Akes, who was reclining upon a pallet upon the floor, slowly and deliberately arose, seemingly indifferent as to whether he got up or not. His manner toward the interviewer, however, was very civil and might even be called pleasant. His replies to interrogatories put to him were prompt and, apparently, without reservation. He denied most emphatically that he attacked the negro man as stated, and accounts for the assertion upon the theory that he was mistaken for some one else.

HIS STORY

of the fight is to the effect that he and his companion were drinking, and visited the house where the difficulty occurred simply "upon a lark." He says that when Mr. Watts approached him he did not know he (Watts) was an officer, and had he been duly apprised of the fact no resistance would have been made. He also said the officer put his hand upon his pistol, which caused him to draw and fire. He says he only shot once, and thought he was acting in self-defense.

It is learned from C. A. McCash, a resident of Adir, Modoc county, who called at this office last evening, that the Vigilantes have been doing some hanging in Big Valley, Lassen county. An old criminal and desperado, by the name of John Adams, a half-breed Mexican, has been hanging around that portion of the country for some time past stealing horses, committing other depressions, and terrorizing the people. That section is very sparsely settled, and the law's protection is a weak arm indeed. The neighbors assembled, held a consultation, and had a committee wait upon him, and ask him to leave that portion of the country. He laughed at the committee, told them there were not enough men in Lassen county to intimidate, nor in the state to hang him. He boldly asserted that he was an outlaw, and recounted many of his thieving exploits in their neighborhood. When the time had elapsed which the committee had given him to make himself scarce, the desperate fellow still remained. The neighbors again assembled last Friday night, and the verdict of all was that he should be lynched. Accordingly they went that night, about 11 o'clock, to where he was known to be stopping, at a house near the banks of Pit river, secreted themselves, some thirty strong, and watched for his appearance. They were not long in waiting, when they saw him passing from the house to the barn. Immediately he was seized by strong and resolute men, bound, conveyed to a convenient oak tree, and with little ceremony John Adams in a few moments was hanging 'by the neck, a lifeless corpse.

LYNCH LAW IN KENTUCKY.
Two Men Hanged by a Mob in Elliott County. [Grayson (Ky.) Cor. Cincinnati Enquirer.]
Two Men Hanged by a Mob in Elliott County. [Grayson (Ky.) Cor. Cincinnati Enquirer.]

Murder, incendiarism, thievery, bushwhacking, general devilment—and such a farce as most of the Kentucky courts prove to be when criminals are brought before them—have at last incited the better citizens of Northeast Kentucky to rise in their might and enforce their will as best they can. In dispatches some weeks since mention was made of an organized band of outlaws in this part of Kentucky, and that a body of masked men had visited Martinsburg, the county seat of Elliott county, and served notices on officers, lawyers, citizens and criminals that they would no longer suffer murderers and known criminals to override and disgrace their county, and that officers and lawyers who gave them encouragement by defending and permitting such persons to go unpunished would be served in the same way as criminals.

On Monday near midnight about 200 men rode into the town of Martinsburg and surrounded the entire court-yard, in which the jail stands, in which John W. Kendall, William McMillan and J. W. Ownsby were confined, charged with various crimes, and known to belong to the organization holding sway in this part of the State. In the meantime part of the regulators surrounded the jailer's house, from which he attempted to escape by a back door, but, in the darkness, ran into the arms of one of the party. They made him deliver the keys to the jail. When they surrounded the court-yard there were several men about the yard with the guards. Among them was John Cohn, whom they caught and tried to secure, but he broke away from them. They fired two shots at him, both of which took effect, one in the left shoulder, the other in the left hip. He finally escaped. They intended to hang him. The party having the jail keys arrived by this time, when about twenty-five proceeded to the jail. Unlocking it, they were met by William McMillan, who began praying for mercy. Kendall was stolid, and made no appeals. Ownsby talked but little, but he was badly frightened, as he had been hanged several times some weeks since by the regulators to make him tell what he knew of the band that he belonged to. Only one man spoke to him. They soon produced ropes and pinioned the arms of Kendall and McMillan, and, leading them to the door, placed the ropes around their necks. They left Ownsby praying for mercy, closed and locked the door, laid the keys by the side of the door, and, without a word being spoken by the whole party of men, filed out of the courtyard and proceeded to a walnut tree about 100 yards from the Court House, where they formed a hollow square about their prisoners and instituted a trial bench. After near an hour the sentence of death was pronounced by Judge Lynch. McMillan begged for a little time to pray, which was granted. A small rope that had evidently been used as a plow-line was used to hang McMillan. When all was ready four strong men caught him and held him up some distance so that one of the party, who climbed the tree, could tie the rope to a limb. They let him down gradually, so as not to break the rope. He was strangled to death. Until this time Kendall had kept quiet. When he saw his partner in the throes of death, he began calling on his God for mercy. His prayers were cut short. He died hard. Both were hanged on the same tree. The regulators remained about half an hour, and quietly left town by another road.

AND LYNCHING.
Louisville, March 10.—A special from Grogson, Ky., says: A another calamity took place in Upper Big Sinking Creek, Carter county, last night. A party of regulators, consisting of one hundred citizens, rode to James Bincen's house and asked for John Boggs, quite a notorious character, who was concealed about the house. Bincen refused to open the door but commenced a fusilade on the regulators, firing 50 shots, and killing, it is believed, one of them. This enraged the regulators, who had come mostly to notify Boggs to leave the country, and in their rage they broke down the doors of the house. It is thought three and a half men who was instantly killed. A rock thrown at the door to break it down hit Bincen's wife and broke her right leg. Thereupon the regulators seized John Boggs and after a short trial took him to a walnut tree standing 15 steps from the house, where they hung him with a cotton rope and then fired two shots at him, one penetrating his body and the other piercing his hand. In this condition Boggs was found this morning by Dr. Steel, who cut the rope and took his corpse to Boggs' family. A nineteen-year old son of Bincen's was taken out and whipped by the regulators for having joined the fusilade against them.

THE ROMANCE OF CRACKER'S NECK.
T COLONEL GEORGE W. SYMONDS.

That turbulent and tortuous stream the Little Sandy river coils itself completely around a rocky plateau of about 10,000 acres area, in the Western corner of Elliott county, Kentucky, the waters of the river being divided by a narrow strip of crumbled cliff. From time immemorial this peninsula has borne the euphoric name of "Cracker's Neck." It is a wild and gloomy spot, if you follow the boundaries of the plateau and view it from the opposite bank of the river. Walled in on all sides by frowning cliffs, rising nearly perpendicular to the height of 300 feet, their upper edge fringed by a heavy growth of stunted firs and laurel bushes, it certainly has a forbidding look. If you have the curiosity to explore the plateau and climb the summit of the crumbling cliff at the point of jointure with the mainland, the aspect changes. Ten years ago there was a thick growth of heavy timber on the "neck," but it has all been cleared away, and a vista of fertile fields and neatly fenced plantations sweep away on all sides to the cliff edges, which are still bordered by the laurel and fir growth. Evidences of civilization in the way of comfortable houses and stables and sheep flocks cropping the succulent herbage are seen on every hand. Immediately after the close of the late war a man named Peter J. Livingstone, who had commanded a regimen of guerrillas on the Confederate side, purchased the neck for a nominal sum, cleared away the timber, laid off fields, built roads and erected houses and opened a store just on the verge of the crumbling cliff, down which you clambered to reach the mainland. He cut down this cliff and graded a road to the farther edge of the plateau, with lateral feeders running off on either side. He brought his family here, installed them in a luxurious home, and began a flourishing business, the basis of which was timber, great tracts of which were owned by him on the mainland. The geographical situation of the "neck" was an admirable one for business purposes, it being a sort of half-way station between the undeveloped riches of wild Kentucky and capital which stretched out eager hands toward the new-old country from the other side of the Ohio river. He speedily drew about him an enormous trade and acted as a factor for the whole of the back country. He was an affable, pleasant-mannered man and made friends.
At this time Mountain Kentucky was in a state of anarchy, Law and order were but little regarded, and the woods were filled with armed men engaged in those terrible family feuds which have made the dark and bloody ground famous. It was the favorite rendezvous, too, for a much worse class of criminals. Thieves and counterfeiters made their headquarters among the wild gorges and deep forests from which they emerged, at frequent intervals, to prey on the fatness of the rich blue-grass country but a few miles distant. Robberies were of frequent occurrence, and stolen horses and cattle were stamped out of the low country by the hundred head. They would be secreted here until the hue and cry was over, and then conveyed across the Ohio river and sold. It was known to the authorities that the desperadoes were well organized, and all efforts to break up the gang were fruitless. During all this time Colonel Peter J. Livingstone flourished and waxed rich, and no one suspected that he had a hand in the lawless acts which were fast driving honest people out of the mountains, and deterring others from coming in to take their places.

Peter J. Livingstone's business prospered so well that it was not long before he had competition. Two Virginians, father and son, named Malone, set up a store on the mainland, directly on the road to Livingstone's store, and much of the trade which hitherto of necessity had gone to him was directed to the new establishment. The falling off in his business enraged Colonel Livingstone beyond measure, and he had an open quarrel with the Malones. After this quarrel the two firms tried to injure each other in the way of trade as much as possible. Livingstone made threats that he would break up the Malones, and drive them from the county. In the spring of 1877 Malone's store was broken into and robbed of several hundred dollars' worth of goods, and Colonel Livingstone gloried in the discomfiture of his rivals over their loss. john-binion-elliott-county-1882-06.A17: The story of this execution, "by command of Judge Lynch," is a brief one. The two secret meetings which had been held by the citizens of Elliott county, were for the purpose of organizing a "society of public protection and justice." One of the most prominet citizens of the county was at its head. Every man of standing, every man who loved order and respected the law in the county enrolled himself in the new order. Its spies were more ubiquitous than the hired detective, and brought to the chief of the order startling intelligence. Livingstone's gang was becoming frightened, and had resolved on heroic measures for the succor of their brethren in durance vile. They had resolved to anticipate the law's slow delay, and rescue their friends by force. At the same time it was intended to burn Martinsburg and shoot down all opposition. The generalissimo of the "Regulators" knew that Peter J. Livingstone was at the head of the order. He had wrung a confirmation of this knowledge from Ormsby and from Kendall and McMillan. He was provided with a list of the members of the gang. The lodge, in solemn conclave, voted to mete out impartial justice to all evil doers. Sentence of death was pronounced on Kendall, McMillan, Livingstone, Lewis Binion, John Binion and John Boggs. Other members of the gang received sentences varying from five to one hundred lashes on the bare back and notice to quit the State. The lodge rode into Martinsburg at midnight, armed and disguised; they forced the jailer to deliver up the keys of the jail, and brought forth Kendall and McMillan to suffer the extreme penalty of lynch law. The frightened wretches confessed everything, implicated Livingstone, the two Binions and Boggs, and were hung up to a walnut tree in the Court House yard. A proclamation was posted in

several prominent places threatening evil doers and their friends and sympathizers with the vengeance of the Regulators.

After hanging the two prisoners the band quietly dispersed. The execution created considerable excitement, but no effort was made to bring the lynchers to justice. The night following they captured Louis Binion and hung him to a ladder set up against his own house. Others of the gang were visited and whipped and ordered to leave the state. For a month the Regulators were every night whipping and hanging. John Binion took to the "bush," and one night endeavored to get out of the county. He and Boggs were to leave together. The latter was a hunter and fisherman, and the place of rendezvous of the two proscribed men was a log cabin which Boggs sometimes occupied on his hunting excursions. The Regulators learned of the movements of the two men and sought to check their flight. They surrounded the cabin and demanded an unconditional surrender. Binion and Boggs refused to give themselves up. The Regulators fired a volley into the cabin, broke down the door, shot Boggs dead and wounded Binion. Binion begged for mercy, but they laughed his prayer to scorn. A rope was placed about his neck, and howling and praying he was dragged to the nearest tree. They strung him up, and as he writhed under the cruel, choking rope, fired a volley into the swinging body and ended the wretch's misery.

The arch criminal Livingstone, however, escaped them. It appears that he learned of the hanging of the two men in Martinsburg and their betrayal of him that same night, and making hasty preparations he fled across the Big Sandy into West Virginia. He remained in hiding for several weeks, wound up his business, collected together all the ready money he could realize and went to Texas, in one of the frontier towns of which state he is now located. The rest of the gang fled the state. A great deal of stolen property was recovered by the detective and returned to the owners. The property on "Cracker's Neck" was divided up and sold by Livingstone's son, after which the young man went to Texas to join his sire.

The new order increased its membership and established subordinate lodges in other counties. It restored order and made law respected. It drove out the desperadoes, thieves and outlaws, and made it possible for an honest man to live in Elliott county. As an evidence of what terror of evil-doing was inspired by the Regulators it is said that a man could lay down a thousand dollars in the middle of the road anywhere in the county and leave it there for weeks without fear of its being picked up, because, as a mountaineer quaintly expressed it to the writer :

"Thar's no tellin', mister, how many rifles mought be coverin' thet same thousand' dollahs, nor how quick a man mought see kingdom kum. Who'd be dratted fool enuff to pick hit up?" —[Detroit Free Press.

LAWLESS DESPERADOES IN LAKE COUNTY.
George Law, who murdered the Calavan boy, on February 13th, about ten miles east of Langell valley, in vicinity of the State line between Modoc and Lake counties, which we mentioned several days ago, is a noted desperado, and chief of the Bonanza Regulators, an organization to prevent settlers from locating in the vicinity of Bonanza. Other persons have been killed suspiciously on former occasions, chargeable to these regulators, who seem to govern that portion of Lake county with as much terror as the cowboys in Arizona. The father of these boys was clubbed sometime ago, and just before an old man was found murdered in his cabin, who had taken up some land for a home. The two boys, when accosted by Law, expected trouble, as threats had been previously made, and the older boy, age 19, had his pistol cocked as quick as Law had his Winchester cocked, both firing instantly, though the younger boy, aged 15, said before his death that Law fired first. Law followed the boys for a fight, as they were not disturbing him, and only looking on the feed grounds for some of their missing cattle. The oldest boy fired his revolver six times at Law, in return for as many rifle shots, and then told his younger brother, who was unarmed, to run his horse at full speed for home, as he had no shots left. As the boy started Law commenced shooting at him, and noticing he was wounded, the older boy sung out to him to let go the bridle rein and hang to the saddle, the latter taking to the brush, as his horse was wounded and unable to travel. The elder Calavan boy felt a bullet pass close by his cheek while in the brush, supposed to be young Law's rifle, and hanging his coat in the brush as a blind he managed to crawl away and escape to his cabin, where the younger brother had pulled off his boots and appeared to be in a dying condition, though able to talk. The elder boy then procured medical assistance from Langell valley, but could not save him. A large posse of citizens, about a dozen or more, headed by the Constable of Bonanza, started to Law's place to arrest him. The Constable thought it best for only three of them to go to Law's place, as he might otherwise show fight. Accordingly they succeeded in making the arrest, but young Law, aged about 20, got the drop on the officer, compelling him to surrender, and, wheeling around quickly, obliged the other two men to do the same. Young Law, assisted by his father and two other persons, after causing the Constable and the two citizens to leave, concluded to follow them, and run them down to where the balance of the citizens were secreted, who, having formed themselves into a circle, succeeded in securing young Law and two other men named Gordon and McKillen, the old man getting away. The elder Law was defiant, and said he would not be taken alive, though it is said he has given himself up, and was bound over by the Bonanza Justice, the others being discharged. There seems to be some doubt whether the murder was committed in Oregon or California. There is a strong feeling against these regulators in both Lake and Modoc counties, and the necks of Law and others will not be safe from Judge Lynch if they can be caught away from their stronghold.—[Yreka Journal, March 8th.

Two laborers named Monahan and MacAvoy quarreled at Steubenville, O., on the 11th inst. The latter was fatally stabbed.

An aged couple named O'Massey, living near Charlottesville, Va., were found murdered on the morning of the 8th inst., in their house. Money was the object.

From fifty to a hundred boats are now engaged in the Straits fisheries, catching an average of twenty to thirty salmon a day. A larger number will soon be employed, and the average catch per boat will be larger during the next two months. —[Contra Costa Gazette.

The farmers in the neighborhood of Vallejo and Benicia are much pleased with the present prospects of large crops. The season was so favorable that almost every available acre of land was put in, and if the weather continues favorable a larger crop will be harvested than ever before. On account of so much land being sown with grain the hay crop will be very short, and it is thought that some of the grain will have to be cut for hay.

The Lakeview (Or.) Examiner says that the men who composed the mob that attempted to lynch Laws at Linkville, and in the melee killed Deputy Sheriff Lewis, are all Lassen county men, and live in and around Beiber and Big Valley. The Examiner gives a detailed account of the fracas, which, if true, shows that the lynchers acted in a cowardly and cold-blooded manner. They all broke and ran for the brush after killing an officer who was powerless in their hands, he at the time he was shot crouching down under cover of a mobber's shotgun.

A meeting of the Seattle, Puget Sound and Gray's Harbor Railroad and Transportation Company was held in Seattle. The President, Governor Newell, and other members of the Board were present. A report was received from the engineer who had made a survey over the proposed route, which represented that the grading and trestle work would be comparatively small. The location of termini on Puget Sound and harbor were not definitely settled. Steilacoom, Johnson's, Dofflamyer's and Brown's points and Olympia were carefully discussed, but no conclusion reached. The road will be about fifty miles in length, passing through one of the very best and most extensive regions of fir, cedar and spruce timber in Washington Territory, along the valley of the Chehalis, well known as one of the most fertile valleys of the Sound country, already highly cultivated and thickly inhabited. It was resolved unanimously to press the enterprise vigorously, and, if possible, to secure an early construction of the road.
laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A26: The people of Lakeview are determined to try and secure the arrest of persons connected with the mob at Linkville. The Commissioners have offered $1,000 reward, and the citizens intend subscribing another $1,000 to secure at least two or more. Should that many be found, it is believed the rest may be found out, all of whom will no doubt be indicted for the murder of Deputy Sheriff Lewis. The Oregonians claim that the mob comprised Californians from Big Valley, and the Big Valley people say they were friends of Laws endeavoring to get Laws from custody under pretense of desiring to lynch him. The latter charge, however, is not generally believed, but it is a matter of doubt whether the mob consisted of Oregonians or Californians, and may have comprised both, as Laws was a terror to the people along the boundary line, where several murders committed are charged to him and the Bonanza regulators, of which organization he was the chief.—[Yreka Journal.

The court, at Harrisburg, Pa., has dissolved nineteen more insurance companies.

The Kansas editorial association is in session at Lawrence, Kan. A large number of editors are present.

Judge Pillsbury, shot by the Chicago riotous mob on the Chicago & Alton road, is improving and recovery is expected.

In Philadelphia, yesterday, a band of counterfeiters were arrested, and a quantity of materials secured. Gopher Bill is among the captured.

F. J. Moses, ex-governor of South Carolina, pleaded guilty in New York, yesterday, to petit larceny, and was sentenced to the penitentiary for six months.

A storm, in Northampton county, North Carolina, yesterday, ruined cotton, wheat and corn crops. Felter's academy, and many other large buildings, were demolished by the winds.

The fiftieth anniversary of the marriage of Harvey Watterson and wife, parents of Henry Watterson, of the Louisville Courier Journal, was celebrated at the latter's residence last evening.

Jos. Marks landed yesterday at St. Johns, N. B. He had been picked up at sea after drifting for four days without food or drink. He was lost from a fishing smack in a fog.

Oscar C. Neal of Oxford, Oakland county, Mich., heretofore convicted in the United States court of pension fraud, yesterday morning was sentenced to the house of correction for seven years.

Louis Manickler, mate of the tug E. M. Peck, and David Plant, fireman, were drowned in the Sault river, Mich., near Sugar island, yesterday, while they were chasing a bear swimming across the river.

The Pittsburgh produce exchange was formally opened yesterday, with appropriate ceremonies. Telegrams of greeting were received from nearly all of the financial produce exchanges throughout the country.

James Winnpenny, of Mansyunk, hung himself yesterday at Philadelphia. He was proprietor of the Arcola mills, employing 120 bands. He was unmarried and eccentric. He leaves an estate valued at $250,000.

John J. Jackson, gubernatorial nominee of the Greenbackers of Delaware, writes that he will not be a figurehead of a farce, and will not accept the nomination unless ratified by respectably sized country meetings.

Ex-Chief Engineer Drake of the Coldwater (Michigan) fire department was held yesterday for trial in the circuit court on the charge of burning buildings last summer so as to prove the efficiency of the fire department.

John Jackson and wife, living at Harris Station, M.O., went to church last Sunday, leaving four children, the eldest fourteen and the youngest two years, in the house; while gone the house and all the children burned.

The Chicago city council has passed an ordinance, mitigating somewhat the severity of the building laws relative to cottages of veneered brick, but there has been such a loud protest from citizens that a reconsideration is in progress.

Four masked men attempted to rob the west bound train on the Union Pacific road near Denton, Texas, yesterday. They flagged the train but suspicion was aroused, and they were put to flight by a volley from passengers' revolvers.

J. W. Goran, (colored), route agent, on the Mississippi & Tennessee railroad, who was arrested April 14, for robbing a registered pouch, at Grenada, Miss., was sentenced yesterday, at Oxford, Miss., to two years in the Chester, Ill., penitentiary.

At Blue Mound, Ill., yesterday, B. F. Scott beat in the skull of his wife with a monkey wrench, because she would not give him money to buy whisky. It is believed she will die. Scott was arrested. They had lived separate for a year.

John W. Wallace, cashier of the Shelbyville, Tennessee, Savings' bank, telegraphs the American that the article in the St. Louis Republican Saturday, charging fraud against the president of the bank in all its material allegations is grossly false.

In a quarrel at Cordington, Ohio, on the Bee line road last evening, Thos. Archer, colored, fired on two men named Sherman and Hayneworth, a shot gun. It is reported that two of the men will die. Archer was arrested and a mob is organizing. It is thought if death results he will be lynched.

A big fire occurred in Rochester, Beaver county, Pa., yesterday, which at one time threatened the entire town. It started in a stove foundry near the depot, and owing to a high wind spread to other shops, factories and offices near by. A hotel was also damaged. Loss, $25,000; insurance, $5,000.

Charles C. Howe, watchman on the propeller City of Rome, was washed overboard Sunday morning about fifteen miles above Long Point, on Lake Erie. The wind blowing a gale, Howe was assisting one of the deck hands at the time. The stupid deck hand did not report the accident till a quarter of an hour afterwards.

The people of Mount Gilead, Ohio, would not address Thomas J. Archer as "Mister Archer," but spoke to and of him familiarly as "Tom." As he is half negro, he resented the lack of deference as a studied insult because of his color, and quarreled with a number of his townsmen. At length his exasperation led him to shoot three of them, though none of them was much hurt. Then a mob tried to breach him, and failing in that, burned all the buildings on his farm.

In common with other businesses auctioneering firms held their own for many a long day in London. When the Duke of Bedford sold out in 1800, on account of pulling down his fine old Inigo Jones mansion, Mr. Christie was the auctioneer.
"London life seems to me," wrote George Ticknor in 1851. "to have become more oppressive than it ever was. The breakfasts that used to be modest reunions of half a dozen, with a dish or two of cold meat, are now dinners in disguise. The lunches are much the same, with several sorts of wine—an advance of luxury which can bode no good to any people." What would Mr. Ticknor have thought of the change which ten years have produced in New York? Luncheons exclusively for ladies nowadays often cost from $15 to $20 a plate.

A Kansas liquor seller, who was sentenced for violation of the prohibition laws to a fine of $100 and costs and thirty days' imprisonment, shot himself shortly after his release from jail. The opponents of the liquor laws say that the man was driven to commit suicide by persecution, and they call him "the seventh victim whom the temperance crew have upon their conscience." The prohibitionists, on the other hand, say that the man's suicide is to be attributed "to mental derangement arising from excessive consumption of alcohol." There is controversy over the case.

thos-archer-cardington-1882-06-06.A9:
He Wanted to be Called Mr.
Mt. Gilead Dispatch to Cincinnati Enquirer.

Thomas J. Archer, a colored citizen of Cardington, Ohio, has for many years been on bad terms with many of his townsmen on account of the refusal on their part to call him Mr. Archer. Yesterday he got into a difficulty with a number of fellows, and the matter was wound up by Archer shooting three persons. A mob was raised and threats of lynching were made by some of the leading citizens. The sheriff and deputy sheriff were called from this city in the evening, and the Levering Guards were in readiness to march upon telegram from Sheriff Modir. At twelve o'clock last night Archer, however, was safely lodged in jail here, the sheriff having secreted his man here for some two hours, fearing a perfectly harmless crowd that had assembled through sheer curiosity around the jail. At about the hour of eleven o'clock a fire was noticed in the direction of Cardington, and it was afterward learned by your correspondent that all of Archer's farm buildings, house, barn, and so forth, had been burned by the excited mob.
